test.name: Dual-dating notation — extract New Style year, no day shift requested
test.description: User supplies a pre-1752 English date in slash notation ('15 February 1750/1') and asks which year to use in their records. The skill should explain that the LATER year is the New Style (modern) year and explicitly stop there — NOT silently apply the 11-day Julian-Gregorian shift the user didn't ask for. Tests restraint and exactly answering the question asked. The date sits inside the 1 January - 24 March double-dating window, where 'use the later year' is unambiguously correct; the boundary day itself is ut_convert_dates_016.

input.user_message: What does '15 February 1750/1' mean on this English marriage record? Which year do I use in my research notes?

judge_context: Should explain dual-dating notation: pre-1752 England began the legal year on 25 March, so dates from 1 January to 24 March were written with both the Old Style and New Style years
Should explain that the later year (1751) is the New Style year and is the year typically used in modern genealogical records, while preserving the original notation in citations

Should NOT apply the Julian-to-Gregorian DAY offset, which would move the day-of-month: '15 February' becoming '26 February 1751' (+11 days) is the failure this bullet looks for, and it is still a failure when hedged as optional, offered as a further step, or framed as what to do 'if correlating with another country'. Resolving the YEAR is NOT that failure — writing '15 February 1750/1 = 15 February 1751', with the day and month unchanged, is the correct answer required by the bullet above and must not be marked down as an unrequested conversion
Should note that the original notation '1750/1' is worth preserving in the source citation
